characters: Rita Mansah: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform, holding a small tree seedling in a polythene bag.
Mr Ohene: the social studies teacher, in a patterned shirt, with a poster of a smiling woman among trees.
Wangari Maathai: a Kenyan scientist and activist (1940–2011), shown in a poster in a bright headwrap, planting a tree with women.
The school compound: a bare yard with red earth, a few seedlings in bags and students with watering cans.

narrationPlan.voice: Eager girl’s voice for Rita; a warm, storytelling voice for Mr Ohene
narrationPlan.pace: Warm and inspiring, with steady pride (about 118 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Gentle East African-style lyre and drums; a rising, hopeful theme (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Rita, Mr Ohene and the school are invented. Wangari Maathai (1940–2011) was a real public figure; the facts are from the Nobel Prize biography and other published sources: born in Nyeri, Kenya, in 1940; first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate (University of Nairobi, 1971); the Green Belt Movement planted trees with women’s groups; she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004 and died on 25 September 2011.

The small payment for each surviving seedling is from the Green Belt Movement’s own website (about US 10 cents, paid to nursery groups) and a YES! Magazine profile (a nominal amount, less than 10 US cents a tree); a figure of 4 Kenyan shillings was suggested in a review but not confirmed, so it is not used. Her Nobel lecture itself says only that the work creates employment.

The number of trees is shown as differing accounts (more than 20 million in the Nobel biography; more than 30 million in her 2004 Nobel lecture; more than 51 million in the Green Belt Movement’s 2011 annual report).

The quotation “plant seeds of peace” is checked against the text of her Nobel lecture (10 December 2004), where it describes people who protect the environment, promote democracy and defend human rights. The payment for surviving seedlings is also in the movement’s 2011 annual report (compensation for seedlings planted and surviving).
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check every date and fact against the Nobel Prize biography and Nobel lecture (nobelprize.org), including what women told Maathai in the 1970s and the payment-per-tree detail.
Check the quotation on page 5 against the Nobel lecture.
Check the biography-paragraph tip against the NaCCA English syllabus.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement told through a Ghanaian class that plants its own trees. It models a biography paragraph in exam-safe English.
learningGoals: Describe how one idea became a movement.
Explain why numbers from different sources can differ.
Write a biography paragraph in the third person and past tense.
beforeReading: Ask: what small thing could you do that, repeated by many people, would matter?
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners how a writer should handle two different numbers.
afterReading: Plant and label a tree with an adult; write a watering rota.
Write a biography paragraph about a local hero.
discussion: Why did Maathai start by listening?
Why did she pay the women for each surviving tree?
reflection: What problem in your community might begin with listening?

mathsExtension.task: A nursery plants 120 seedlings and 3 out of 4 survive. How many survive?
Suppose a class waters each of its 12 seedlings with 2 litres of water a day, how many litres does it use a day?

support: Provide a biography frame: Born… Studied… Later… Achieved… Remembered for…
stretch: Write a biography of a Ghanaian environmental or community leader, using at least two sources.

localiseThis: Plant native trees chosen with a local forestry or agriculture officer; do not plant invasive species.

factCheck.claim: Wangari Maathai was born in Nyeri, Kenya, in 1940; earned a doctorate from the University of Nairobi in 1971, the first woman in East and Central Africa to do so; led a tree-planting movement through women’s groups that planted more than 20 million trees (other sources say about 30 million); won the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize; and died on 25 September 2011.
factCheck.explanation: From the Nobel Prize’s biographical note; the tree number is given as a range because sources differ.
